newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU struggles to find a common diplomacy.
newsitem.headline: EU struggles to find a common diplomacy.

text.p: When U.S. President Bill Clinton decided to attack Iraq last week, he telephoned the British prime minister and the French president -- so much for a unified European Union foreign policy.
Britain supported Washington. France objected. Not for the first time, the EU was unable to present a common front.

Despite much talk and a provision in the Maastricht treaty establishing a Common Foreign and Security Policy (CFSP), the 15 nations of the Union are still far from speaking with one voice in world affairs.
On Iraq, they were even unable to agree on a formal CFSP statement.

The disagreement over Washington's action in Iraq, which extended beyond France and Britain and is sure to continue if the United States relaunches its attacks, was only the latest in a series of events in which EU diplomacy has appeared in disarray.
Diplomats say France, in particular, has put strains on the EU's attempts to present a unified front, despite being one of the countries most keen on a stronger CFSP.
Since coming to power last year, President Jacques Chirac has sought a greater world role for France, launching high-profile policies with or without the support of his EU partners.

This included infuriating most of the EU by unilaterally resuming nuclear weapons testing and irritating the then Italian EU presidency by seeking a peace settlement in Lebanon without coordinating the move with Rome.
Dominique Moisi, deputy director of the French Institute for International Relations (IRI), sees such unilateral actions as a reflection of the weakness of pan-European foreign policy.

"If you try to do (something) unilaterally you are immediately accused of damaging the European spirit. But if you try to respect the European spirit, (the policy) becomes so watered down that nothing happens," he said.
Moisi said France had no choice but to act alone in Lebanon if it wanted anything to be achieved.
"There was no way the French could work within European institutions," he said.
Moisi said that Britain and France in particular are resistant to losing control over foreign affairs.

"Deep down, when it comes to foreign policy, both the British and French believe the 'blood tax' cannot be shared," he said, referring to the idea of soldiers shedding blood for a policy decided by other governments.

Added John Roper, associate fellow at Chatham House, the Royal Institute of International Affairs in London: "France, like Britain, makes it very clear that they never see a CFSP replacing a national foreign policy."
One of the main barriers to CFSP lies in the different views of the use of power in Europe's capitals.

Britain and France tend to see foreign policy mainly in historic and military terms, while for Germany power is a matter of economics. Other EU countries, lacking any world role, see pooling their resources as a way of having some power.
"The problem with Europe is that everyone wants to share what it does not have," Moisi said.
Seeking to match its economic weight with equivalent political clout, the EU has been looking at ways to strengthen CFSP as part of the inter-governmental conference (IGC).

British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said at an informal foreign ministers meeting in Tralee, Ireland, on Sunday that the CFSP dossier was one of the areas where IGC negotiators had made most progress.
The main idea to emerge so far -- and approved by all member countries -- is to create a forward planning unit in Brussels that would study issues to help EU states to forge common positions.
"We do have more weight when we can speak as one," Chatham House's Roper said.

No one expects such a body to replace national capitals as the centre of foreign diplomacy, but it is argued that, in situations such as Iraq, the EU would know where its interests lay the moment a crisis erupted.
Differences remain, however, over who should run such a body. Paris is actively arguing for the appointment of a "Mr or Ms CFSP", a top-ranking person whom Clinton could call in an emergency.
France wants the appointee to report directly to the European Council.

Germany prefers someone a bit less high-profile, at secretary general level, who would report to the General Affairs Council. Britain would be happy with a relatively low-level administrative secretary general.
But while such differences and larger foreign policy disagreements can lead some to pronounce CFSP a failure, others say limited EU diplomacy is not only possible but a reality.

"On the one hand the advocates of the CFSP overstate what it can do, on the other hand there is a risk in going the other way and saying it can do nothing," said John Roper of Britain's Royal Institute of International Affairs.
Roper and others say regular meetings of foreign ministers and agreements that have been reached on less divisive issues put the EU light years ahead of where it used to be.
But a strong, common stance with which to address the world?
"If you are not too ambitious, you may be satisfied," IRI's Moisi said.
